Vicious
vĭsh´ŭs
adj. (given to vice; corrupt in nature or habit; faulty at the root)
Latin vitiosus, faulty, from vitium, a defect. The older English sense is nearer to defective than to savage: a vicious argument is one with a flaw in it, and a vicious nature is one with a flaw in it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Vicious describes a nature faulty at the root, and Scripture's figure for it is a tree: “a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit” (Mat 7:17–18). The diagnosis is comprehensive: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9); “there is none righteous, no, not one” (Rom 3:10). And the remedy is at the root: “make the tree good, and his fruit good” (Mat 12:33).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines vicious as defective; faulty; not correct or pure; addicted to vice; corrupt in principles or conduct; and, of the will, depraved.

expand to see more

VICIOUS, a. Defective; imperfect; as a vicious concord in music.

2. Addicted to vice; corrupt in principles or conduct; depraved; wicked; habitually transgressing the moral law.

3. Corrupt; contrary to moral principles or to rectitude; as vicious examples.

4. Foul; impure; as vicious air.

Key Scripture

Mat 7:17 — "Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit."

Mat 7:18 — "A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit."

Jer 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

Rom 3:10 — "As it is written, There is none righteous, no, not one:"

Mat 12:33 — "Either make the tree good, and his fruit good; or else make the tree corrupt, and his fruit corrupt: for the tree is known by his fruit."

Modern Corruption

Bad conduct is treated as behaviour to be corrected, and the Lord's figure puts the fault in the tree.

expand to see more

Matthew 7:18 states an impossibility in both directions: a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. That is stronger than a tendency, and it is the sentence behind the Reformed doctrine of total depravity — which has never meant that men are as bad as they could be, but that no part of the nature is undamaged, so that even the fruit that looks good is growing on a tree with a fault in it. The old word vicious carries this better than the modern one, because it means defective before it means savage.

The consequence for method is exact and unpopular. If the fault is in the tree, then behaviour modification is fruit-tying — the practice of wiring good fruit onto a bad tree, which produces an impressive display for one season and no crop. Matthew 12:33 gives the alternative in four words: make the tree good. Only one agent in the universe can do that, and He does it by a new birth rather than by instruction; which is why the New Testament's ethical commands all come after an indicative about what has been done to the reader, and never before.

There is a use of the doctrine that is itself vicious, and it is to make depravity an excuse: I cannot help it, the tree is what it is. Scripture never allows the inability to reduce the obligation — the same Lord who said the corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit commanded men to repent and believe, and held them responsible for not doing it. The inability is moral, not physical: a man does not lack the faculties to obey, he lacks the will, and a will that will not is guilty in a way that a hand that cannot is not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sapros (G4550), rotten, corrupt; poneros (G4190), evil; Hebrew anash (H605), incurable, desperately wicked; aqob (H6121), deceitful, crooked.

expand to see more

Greek sapros (G4550) — corrupt, rotten; Matthew 7:17–18, 12:33, Ephesians 4:29.

Hebrew aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked; Jeremiah 17:9, with anash (H605), desperately sick.

Greek ouk estin dikaios (G1342) — there is none righteous; Romans 3:10, quoting Psalm 14:1–3.

Usage

"“A corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit” — and cannot do otherwise."

"“Make the tree good, and his fruit good” — the alternative to wiring fruit on."

"“The heart is deceitful above all things” — the fault located."
